```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(nlmixr2lib)
library(PKNCA)
library(rxode2)
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

# Model and source

* Citation: `r rxode2::rxode(readModelDb("Tan_2025_pazopanib"))$reference`
* Article: <https://doi.org/10.1007/s40262-025-01504-5> (open access)

Tan et al. analysed routine therapeutic-drug-monitoring (TDM) data from adults
treated with oral pazopanib at Leiden University Medical Center. They built
three linked models, packaged here as four files:

| Model file | Content |
|------------|---------|
| `Tan_2025_pazopanib` | One-compartment population PK with a dose-nonlinear relative bioavailability |
| `Tan_2025_pazopanib_livertox` | Gompertz time-to-first-event model for CTCAE grade >= 2 liver toxicity, with a step increase in hazard while the trough exceeds 34 mg/L |
| `Tan_2025_pazopanib_tumor_mrcc` | Tumor size (sum of longest diameters, SLD) model for metastatic renal cell carcinoma (mRCC) |
| `Tan_2025_pazopanib_tumor_sts` | The same tumor size structure fitted separately to soft tissue sarcoma (STS) |

The PK model supplies the daily trough concentration (`CTROUGH`) that drives
the liver-toxicity hazard. The tumor models have no exposure dependence: the
authors tested trough, Cmax and dose on the decay rate and kept none of them.

# Population

132 unique patients (93 mRCC, 39 STS) were treated between 2014 and 2023.
Patients who interrupted pazopanib for more than 6 months were entered twice,
which gives 135 "individuals" (96 mRCC, 39 STS; Table 1). Median age was 67
years (range 21-89), median weight 79 kg (45-130), and 50 of 135 were female.
The median starting dose was 800 mg once daily (range 200-800) and the median
dose during treatment 600 mg (200-1000), taken fasted. Race was not reported.

* PK: 460 plasma concentrations (326 troughs, sampled 20-28 h after the dose),
  median 3 per patient.
* Liver toxicity: 27 of 135 patients (20%) had a grade >= 2 ALT, AST or
  alkaline phosphatase elevation within 1 year.
* Tumor size: 111 patients had a baseline SLD and at least one on-treatment CT
  scan (403 SLD records: 322 mRCC, 81 STS). Median baseline SLD was 79 mm in
  mRCC and 88 mm in STS.

The same information is available programmatically via
`readModelDb("Tan_2025_pazopanib")()$population` (and the three companion
files).

# Source trace

Every `ini()` value carries an in-file comment pointing to its source. The
supplement prints all four NONMEM control streams, which confirm the
structures and the final values.

| STS resistant fraction | 0.134 | Table 4; control stream `P(1)` = 0.866 |

# Pharmacokinetics

## Virtual cohort and simulation

Figure 4a of the paper compares three fixed starting regimens: 400, 600 and
800 mg once daily. The cohort below has 200 subjects per regimen, dosed for a
full year so the same simulation also supplies the daily troughs for the
liver-toxicity model. Concentrations are sampled just before each dose (the
daily trough) and hourly over days 29-30 for the steady-state profile.

```{r pk-events}
n_per_arm <- 200L
doses <- c(400, 600, 800)
n_days <- 365L

make_pk_arm <- function(dose, id_offset) {
  ids <- id_offset + seq_len(n_per_arm)
  dose_rows <- data.frame(
    id = ids, time = 0, amt = dose, evid = 1L, cmt = "depot",
    ii = 24, addl = n_days - 1L
  )
  obs_times <- sort(unique(c(
    24 * seq_len(n_days) - 0.01, # daily troughs, just before the next dose
    seq(696, 720, by = 1) # day 29-30 steady-state profile
  )))
  obs_rows <- expand.grid(id = ids, time = obs_times) |>
    mutate(amt = 0, evid = 0L, cmt = "central", ii = 0, addl = 0L)
  bind_rows(dose_rows, obs_rows) |>
    mutate(DOSE = dose, arm = paste(dose, "mg QD")) |>
    arrange(id, time, desc(evid))
}

pk_events <- bind_rows(
  make_pk_arm(400, 0L),
  make_pk_arm(600, n_per_arm),
  make_pk_arm(800, 2L * n_per_arm)
)
stopifnot(!anyDuplicated(unique(pk_events[, c("id", "time", "evid")])))
```

```{r pk-sim}
mod_pk <- readModelDb("Tan_2025_pazopanib")
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20250425)
pk_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_pk, events = pk_events, keep = "arm") |>
  as.data.frame()
```

## Steady-state profiles (Figure 4a)

```{r fig4a, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 6}
pk_ss <- pk_sim |>
  filter(time >= 600, time <= 720) |>
  group_by(arm, time) |>
  summarise(
    med = median(Cc), lo = quantile(Cc, 0.05), hi = quantile(Cc, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ggplot(pk_ss, aes(time / 24, med)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 20.5, linetype = "dashed", colour = "blue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 34, linetype = "dashed", colour = "red") +
  facet_wrap(~arm, ncol = 1) +
  labs(
    x = "Time (day)", y = "Pazopanib concentration (mg/L)",
    caption = "Replicates Figure 4a of Tan 2025: median and 90% prediction interval."
  )
```

The paper states that the 600 mg regimen keeps the steady-state trough at or
above the 20.5 mg/L efficacy threshold in 76% of simulated individuals.

```{r trough-target}
trough_ss <- pk_sim |>
  filter(abs(time - (30 * 24 - 0.01)) < 1e-6) |>
  group_by(arm) |>
  summarise(
    `Median trough (mg/L)` = signif(median(Cc), 3),
    `Trough >= 20.5 mg/L (%)` = round(100 * mean(Cc >= 20.5)),
    `Trough > 34 mg/L (%)` = round(100 * mean(Cc > 34)),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) |>
  rename(Regimen = arm)
knitr::kable(trough_ss, caption = "Simulated day-30 trough by regimen.")
pct_600 <- trough_ss$`Trough >= 20.5 mg/L (%)`[trough_ss$Regimen == "600 mg QD"]
# A cohort-level proportion of 200 subjects (binomial SE about 3 points); the
# bounds catch a wrong F1 exponent or CL, which move it by tens of points.
stopifnot(pct_600 > 60, pct_600 < 95)
```

The simulated proportion at 600 mg (`r pct_600`%) is close to the 76%
the paper reports. The simulated median troughs are about 21, 26 and 31 mg/L
for 400, 600 and 800 mg. Read from Figure 4a, the published medians are about
21, 28 and 30 mg/L, with the 600 and 800 mg curves nearly overlapping. Because
bioavailability falls with dose as `(200 / DOSE)^0.42`, doubling the dose from
400 to 800 mg raises exposure by only about 50%.

## PKNCA validation

The paper reports no NCA, so the check is against the closed form. At steady
state the AUC over one dosing interval is `F * Dose / (CL/F)`, with
`F = (200 / Dose)^0.42`. The typical-value simulation (random effects zeroed)
must reproduce it.

```{r pknca}
pk_typ_events <- bind_rows(lapply(seq_along(doses), function(i) {
  make_pk_arm(doses[i], (i - 1L) * n_per_arm) |> filter(id == min(id))
}))
pk_typ <- rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_pk), events = pk_typ_events, keep = "arm") |>
  as.data.frame()

conc_df <- pk_typ |>
  filter(time >= 696, time <= 720, !is.na(Cc)) |>
  mutate(treatment = arm) |>
  select(id, time, Cc, treatment)
# The interval dose is the one given at 696 h (start of day 30).
dose_df <- pk_typ_events |>
  filter(evid == 1) |>
  transmute(id, time = 696, amt, treatment = arm)

conc_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAconc(conc_df, Cc ~ time | treatment + id)
dose_obj <- PKNCA::PKNCAdose(dose_df, amt ~ time | treatment + id)
intervals <- data.frame(start = 696, end = 720, auclast = TRUE, cmax = TRUE, cmin = TRUE, tmax = TRUE)
nca_res <- PKNCA::pk.nca(PKNCA::PKNCAdata(conc_obj, dose_obj, intervals = intervals))

nca_tab <- as.data.frame(nca_res$result) |>
  select(treatment, PPTESTCD, PPORRES) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = PPTESTCD, values_from = PPORRES) |>
  mutate(
    dose = as.numeric(sub(" mg QD", "", treatment)),
    auc_closed = (200 / dose)^0.42 * dose / 0.497,
    pct_diff = 100 * (auclast / auc_closed - 1)
  )
nca_tab |>
  transmute(
    Regimen = treatment,
    "Cmax (mg/L)" = signif(cmax, 3),
    "Tmax (h)" = signif(tmax, 3),
    "Cmin (mg/L)" = signif(cmin, 3),
    "AUCtau PKNCA (mg*h/L)" = signif(auclast, 4),
    "AUCtau closed form (mg*h/L)" = signif(auc_closed, 4),
    "Difference (%)" = round(pct_diff, 2)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = "Typical-value steady-state NCA (day 29-30) versus the closed form.")
# Same parameters on both sides: the difference is trapezoid error on an
# hourly grid only.
stopifnot(all(abs(nca_tab$pct_diff) < 2))
```

# Liver toxicity

## Closed-form check

With a constant trough the Gompertz cumulative hazard has a closed form,
`H(t) = lambda * RF / shape * (exp(shape * t) - 1)`, with `RF = exp(1.21)`
above 34 mg/L and 1 otherwise. The model must reproduce it exactly.

```{r tox-closed}
mod_tox <- readModelDb("Tan_2025_pazopanib_livertox")
tox_check_events <- expand.grid(id = 1:2, time = seq(0, 365, by = 5)) |>
  mutate(evid = 0L, CTROUGH = ifelse(id == 1, 25, 40)) |>
  arrange(id, time)
tox_check <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_tox, events = tox_check_events, keep = "CTROUGH") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  mutate(
    rf = ifelse(CTROUGH > 34, exp(1.21), 1),
    sur_closed = exp(-0.0021 * rf / -0.012 * (exp(-0.012 * time) - 1))
  )
stopifnot(max(abs(tox_check$sur - tox_check$sur_closed)) < 1e-5)
tox_check |>
  filter(time == 365) |>
  transmute(
    "Constant trough (mg/L)" = CTROUGH,
    "Toxicity-free survival at 365 days" = signif(sur, 3),
    "Closed form" = signif(sur_closed, 3)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

The two constant-trough curves are the typical-value counterparts of the
survival VPC in Figure 1. Below the cutoff the model gives 84% toxicity-free
survival at one year, which matches the observed Kaplan-Meier curve in
Figure 1a (about 84%). Above the cutoff it gives 56%, inside the wide
prediction interval of Figure 1b, where the observed curve ends near 42% after
a small number of patients.

## Toxicity probability by starting dose (Figure 4b)

Each simulated subject's daily trough from the PK simulation above is passed
to the toxicity model as the time-varying `CTROUGH` column. The trough
recorded on day `d` is the concentration just before the dose that starts
day `d + 1`.

```{r tox-sim}
tox_events <- pk_sim |>
  filter(abs(time - (24 * round(time / 24) - 0.01)) < 1e-6) |>
  transmute(id, arm, time = round(time / 24) - 1, CTROUGH = Cc, evid = 0L) |>
  filter(time >= 0, time <= 365) |>
  arrange(id, time)
tox_sim <- rxode2::rxSolve(mod_tox, events = tox_events, keep = "arm") |>
  as.data.frame()

tox_curve <- tox_sim |>
  group_by(arm, time) |>
  summarise(prob_tox = 1 - mean(sur), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(tox_curve, aes(time, prob_tox, colour = arm)) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    x = "Time (day)", y = "Probability of grade >= 2 liver toxicity", colour = NULL,
    caption = "Replicates Figure 4b of Tan 2025 (expected cumulative incidence)."
  )

tox_365 <- tox_curve |>
  filter(time == max(time)) |>
  mutate(published = c(0.21, 0.16, 0.37)[match(arm, paste(doses, "mg QD"))])
tox_365 |>
  transmute(
    Regimen = arm,
    "Simulated probability at 1 year" = round(prob_tox, 3),
    "Figure 4b (read from plot)" = published
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
p_tox <- setNames(tox_365$prob_tox, tox_365$arm)
# Expected (not event-sampled) incidence over 200 subjects: monotone in dose
# and bounded by the two constant-trough closed forms (0.16 and 0.44).
stopifnot(
  p_tox[["800 mg QD"]] > p_tox[["600 mg QD"]],
  p_tox[["600 mg QD"]] > p_tox[["400 mg QD"]],
  all(p_tox > 0.15), all(p_tox < 0.45)
)
```

The simulated one-year risks at 400 and 600 mg are close to the published
values (within about 0.07), but the 800 mg risk is lower than the published 0.37,
and the published order of 400 mg (0.21) above 600 mg (0.16) is not
reproduced. The packaged model cannot reach 0.37 at 800 mg with these
troughs. Even a subject whose trough stays above 34 mg/L for the whole year
has a one-year risk of only 0.44 (the closed-form check above), so 0.37 would
need roughly three quarters of the cohort above the cutoff. The paper's own
Figure 4a puts the 800 mg median trough near 30 mg/L, which means fewer than
half of the subjects are above 34 mg/L. Passing the troughs with their PK
residual error (the `sim` column) as `CTROUGH` raises the 800 mg risk by
only about 0.01. The model hazard rises with the trough and the
trough rises with the dose, so the published 400 / 600 mg inversion points to
Monte Carlo noise in the paper's event-sampled curves. The parameters were
not adjusted to close these gaps.

# Tumor size

## Closed-form check

The tumor ODE is linear in SLD, so for fixed parameters
`log(SLD(t) / SLD(0)) = p * t - kkill / res * (1 - exp(-res * t))`, with
`kkill = 0` in the primary-resistant class. The relative change does not
depend on the baseline SLD.

```{r tumor-closed}
mod_mrcc <- readModelDb("Tan_2025_pazopanib_tumor_mrcc")
mod_sts <- readModelDb("Tan_2025_pazopanib_tumor_sts")
tumor_check_events <- expand.grid(id = 1:2, time = seq(0, 360, by = 30)) |>
  mutate(evid = 0L, cmt = "tumor_size", TUM_SLD = 80, MIX_PRIM_RESIST = id - 1L) |>
  arrange(id, time)
closed_pct <- function(time, p, kkill, res, resist) {
  100 * (exp(p * time - (1 - resist) * kkill / res * (1 - exp(-res * time))) - 1)
}
tumor_check <- bind_rows(
  rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_mrcc), events = tumor_check_events, keep = "MIX_PRIM_RESIST") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(tumor = "mRCC", closed = closed_pct(time, 0.0005, 0.004, 0.008, MIX_PRIM_RESIST)),
  rxode2::rxSolve(rxode2::zeroRe(mod_sts), events = tumor_check_events, keep = "MIX_PRIM_RESIST") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(tumor = "STS", closed = closed_pct(time, 0.0086, 0.008, 0.0003, MIX_PRIM_RESIST))
) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (tumor_size / 80 - 1))
stopifnot(max(abs(tumor_check$pct - tumor_check$closed)) < 0.01)
tumor_check |>
  filter(time == 360) |>
  transmute(
    Tumor = tumor,
    Class = ifelse(MIX_PRIM_RESIST == 1, "primary resistant", "primary sensitive"),
    "SLD change at day 360 (%)" = round(pct, 1)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

## Population tumor size over time (Figure 4c)

Figure 4c shows the median and 90% prediction interval of the SLD change from
baseline. Its curves match the **primary-sensitive** class rather than the
full mixture:

* The mRCC median ends near -22% and the band tops out near 0%.
* The STS median ends between +30% and +60% (one curve per dose, which
  differ only by Monte Carlo noise) and the band reaches about +165%.

A primary-resistant STS subject grows more than 20-fold in a year (the
closed-form table above). With 13.4% of the cohort in that class, the 95th
percentile of a full-mixture simulation would lie far above +165%. The cohort
below therefore simulates 200 sensitive subjects per tumor type with full
inter-individual variability for the comparison, and a second cohort with the
class drawn from a Bernoulli distribution with the Table 4 probability (0.27
mRCC, 0.134 STS) shows the full mixture. Baseline SLD is drawn log-normally
around the Table 1 medians. It does not affect the percentage change, but it
makes the absolute SLD realistic.

```{r tumor-sim, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 5}
set.seed(20250425)
make_tumor_cohort <- function(p_resist, sld_median) {
  subj <- data.frame(
    id = seq_len(n_per_arm),
    MIX_PRIM_RESIST = rbinom(n_per_arm, 1, p_resist),
    TUM_SLD = sld_median * exp(rnorm(n_per_arm, 0, 0.6))
  )
  expand.grid(id = subj$id, time = seq(0, 360, by = 10)) |>
    left_join(subj, by = "id") |>
    mutate(evid = 0L, cmt = "tumor_size") |>
    arrange(id, time)
}
sim_tumor <- function(mod, events, tumor, population) {
  rxode2::rxSolve(mod, events = events, keep = "TUM_SLD") |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    mutate(tumor = tumor, population = population)
}
rxode2::rxSetSeed(20250425)
tumor_sim <- bind_rows(
  sim_tumor(mod_mrcc, make_tumor_cohort(0, 79), "mRCC", "Primary sensitive"),
  sim_tumor(mod_sts, make_tumor_cohort(0, 88), "STS", "Primary sensitive"),
  sim_tumor(mod_mrcc, make_tumor_cohort(0.27, 79), "mRCC", "Full mixture"),
  sim_tumor(mod_sts, make_tumor_cohort(0.134, 88), "STS", "Full mixture")
) |>
  mutate(pct = 100 * (tumor_size / TUM_SLD - 1))

tumor_summ <- tumor_sim |>
  group_by(population, tumor, time) |>
  summarise(
    med = median(pct), lo = quantile(pct, 0.05), hi = quantile(pct, 0.95),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
ggplot(
  tumor_summ |> filter(population == "Primary sensitive"),
  aes(time, med)
) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-30, 20), linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~tumor, ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(
    x = "Time (day)", y = "SLD change from baseline (%)",
    caption = paste(
      "Replicates Figure 4c of Tan 2025 (primary-sensitive class):",
      "median and 90% prediction interval."
    )
  )

tab_360 <- tumor_summ |>
  filter(time == 360) |>
  arrange(tumor, desc(population))
tab_360 |>
  transmute(
    Tumor = tumor,
    Population = population,
    "Median (%)" = round(med),
    "5th percentile (%)" = round(lo),
    "95th percentile (%)" = round(hi)
  ) |>
  knitr::kable(caption = paste(
    "SLD change from baseline at day 360. Figure 4c shows a median near -22%",
    "(band about -35% to 0%) for mRCC and +30% to +60% (band about -35% to",
    "+165%) for STS."
  ))
med_sens <- tab_360 |> filter(population == "Primary sensitive")
med_mrcc <- med_sens$med[med_sens$tumor == "mRCC"]
med_sts <- med_sens$med[med_sens$tumor == "STS"]
# Medians of 200 subjects; the bounds bracket the Figure 4c medians and still
# separate shrinkage (mRCC) from growth (STS), which a swapped or
# mis-transcribed rate would reverse.
stopifnot(med_mrcc < -10, med_mrcc > -40, med_sts > 20, med_sts < 80)
```

The sensitive-class medians reproduce Figure 4c. In mRCC the median tumor
shrinks and then levels off, because the drug-induced decay wanes with an
acquired-resistance half-life of about 87 days (`log(2) / 0.008`). In STS the
growth rate is already higher than the decay rate at the start, so the median
tumor grows throughout the year. The simulated mRCC 90% band is much wider
than the published one, mainly from the 130% CV on the growth rate KG. The
published band is narrower than that IIV implies, so the paper's simulation
may not have sampled every random effect; the paper does not say. Including
the primary-resistant class moves the mRCC median towards no change, and
stretches the STS upper tail to the resistant class's twenty-fold growth. The authors simulated all three starting doses with the same
tumor model, because the model has no exposure dependence.

# Assumptions and deviations

* **IIV variances.** Tables 2 and 4 report inter-individual variability as
  `CV% = sqrt(omega)`. The control-stream `$OMEGA` values confirm this: 0.58
  gives 76.2% against the printed 76.5%, and 1.69 gives 130%. The variances
  in the model files are the squared table values (for STS `IIV_KD`, the
  control-stream value 0.017).
* **No IIV on CL/F.** The Results text says IIV on CL/F, V/F and F1 were
  estimated, but Table 2 and the control stream contain IIV only on V/F and F1
  (`CL = THETA(1)`). The model follows the table and the control stream.
* **Table 2 units.** Table 2 labels `Ka` in "h"; the unit is 1/h (Ozbey 2021
  reports 0.976 1/h).
* **Toxicity model has no residual error.** The TTE model was fitted by
  likelihood with no random effects (`$OMEGA 0 FIX` on lambda). The
  `addSd_sur` placeholder is fixed to 0.001 so the model compiles; it is not
  from the paper.
* **Cutoff direction.** The Results text says ">= 34 mg/L" in one place and
  the abstract and control stream say "> 34". The model uses the control
  stream (`trough.GT.34`).
* **Trough input.** The paper derived the daily trough from each patient's
  empirical-Bayes PK parameters and real dosing history. Here it comes from
  simulated PK subjects on fixed regimens without TDM dose adjustment.
* **Mixture class as a covariate.** The NONMEM `$MIXTURE` class is supplied as
  the binary column `MIX_PRIM_RESIST`. Its population probability (0.27 mRCC,
  0.134 STS) is documented in `covariateData` rather than carried as an
  `ini()` parameter, and must be drawn per subject for population simulation.
* **Tumor-model populations.** The paper does not split the 111 tumor-size
  patients by tumor type, so the demographic fields of the two tumor files
  describe the whole mRCC and STS PK cohorts. Table 1 lists 69 male / 30
  female in the mRCC column, which sums to 99 rather than 96; the female share
  is computed from those printed counts.
* **Figure readings.** The Figure 4 comparison values were read from the plot
  by eye; they are approximate.
* **Figure 4c population.** The paper does not say which subpopulation Figure
  4c shows. The published medians and bands match the primary-sensitive class
  (see the tumor section), so that class is the comparison here.
